title: Turn one real customer project into useful website content
description: A practical way for Okanagan and other small businesses to turn one real customer project into useful website content, photography, service pages, and video without inventing proof.
summary: Start with permission, a clear brief, the problem, constraints, work, and results. Use real images and honest wording. Then decide whether the project belongs on a service page, a local page, a case study, video, or social content. One well handled project can support the next sales conversation.
takeaways: Get permission and agree on the brief before photographing or publishing customer work.
Use real images, exact project constraints, and honest results instead of invented reviews.
Choose the right home for the story: service page, local page, standalone case study, video, or social.
Treat one project as reusable source material, but do not claim broader results than the work can support.

sections.title: Start with permission, not a publish button
sections.body:
The useful version of this content starts with a real project and a real conversation. Before photos, captions, page copy, or a video call go anywhere near your website, the customer should know what you want to show, where it might appear, and what details you would rather not publish. That protects trust and usually makes the content better, because both sides can think about what is genuinely useful instead of trying to hide a vague story.

It also helps to agree on the brief before anyone starts polishing anything. What problem did the customer bring to you? What limits were in place? What work did you actually do? What happened afterwards? For a business owner thinking about marketing and branding help, that is the practical centre of the job. A glossy project story that dodges those questions rarely persuades anybody who is close to buying.

For example, suppose a landscaping company finished a spring cleanup in West Kelowna and the client mentioned that the phone started ringing more often after the site was updated. That is useful, but it is not the same thing as a universal result. The business can discuss what changed in qualified bookings for that work, while still being clear that the project does not prove every similar website will do the same.

sections.title: Write the brief before you write the case study
sections.body:
A good customer project page starts with the problem in plain language. Then it gives the constraint. Then it shows the work. Then it describes the result. That sounds obvious, but a lot of websites jump straight to praise, adjectives, or a screenshot, and the reader still has no idea what was difficult, what changed, or why the project matters.

A simple brief can keep you honest:

Project: replace a dated service page and add clearer local information.
Problem: visitors could not tell whether the business served their area, what the service included, or what to ask first.
Constraint: limited photography, one busy owner, and no appetite for a long monthly marketing programme.
Work: clarified the offer, rebuilt the page, added local detail, improved forms and calls to action.
Result: the owner reported more consistent enquiries and better fit after launch.

That kind of brief is more useful than a paragraph of inflated praise. It gives the next owner something to compare with their own situation. If you are also thinking about broader website design and development, the same brief helps you decide what content deserves space on the site and what is just noise.

sections.title: Use the real work, not a polished fiction
sections.body:
Real images beat generic stock because they show judgement. A photo of the yard before the work started, a shot of the service van in a real neighbourhood, a screenshot of the old page, or a short clip from the job can all carry more weight than a stack of invented five star reviews. People can tell when the proof has been sanded into something too smooth. A little reality is often more persuasive.

That does not mean publishing every unflattering detail. It means using the project to show how you think. What did you notice? What was not worth changing? What had to be handled carefully? A good piece of project content can show taste, restraint, and a working brain at the same time. For many small businesses, that is exactly what brand and content work should do: help a buyer see the difference between a pretty page and useful judgement.

If you have customer photos or a testimonial, use them carefully. Do not put words in somebody's mouth. Do not make a review do more work than it actually did. And do not imply a measured result unless you have one. An owner in Kelowna or Vernon does not need theatre. They need enough truth to make a sensible call.

sections.title: Choose the right place for the story
sections.body:
Not every customer project needs its own long case study page. Sometimes the strongest use is a section on an existing service page. Sometimes it belongs on a local page because the neighbourhood, climate, building stock, or seasonal timing changed the job. Sometimes it works better as a short article, a few image captions, or a video with one clean point. The right home depends on what the reader needs next.

A service page is a good place for proof when the project shows a repeatable part of your offer. A local page is better when the value depends on the area, the housing style, the soil, the lot shape, the water pressure, the appliance brand, or some other local detail. A standalone case study is better when the project has enough depth to reward a slower read. If you already have a broad site, it may make sense to fold the story into a stronger local service page system rather than piling on another page.

For example, suppose an appliance repair business wants to show that it handles refrigerators, dishwashers, and cooking appliances across the Okanagan and Shuswap. A few real project notes on the relevant service pages will usually work harder than a generic portfolio page. The visitor is already looking for a specific fix. Let the project answer that exact question.

sections.title: Turn one project into video and social without stretching it
sections.body:
One real project can produce several useful pieces of content if you plan it that way. A short video can show the problem, the work, and the result in a way a paragraph cannot. A few stills can support a service page. One thoughtful social post can tell the customer story without turning into an ad for yourself. The point is not to multiply content for its own sake. It is to make one honest project easier to understand from different angles.

If you want video, plan for accessibility and clarity rather than only atmosphere. The W3C guidance on accessible audio and video is useful here because it pushes you to think about captions, transcripts, clear audio, and how people actually experience the clip. That matters even more when the project involves a client speaking to camera. Good video is not just a glossy ad. It helps people understand what happened and what they might reasonably ask next.

Social content works best when it respects the same rule. Do not squeeze a one week project into a life changing saga. If the customer is happy for you to show the work, show it plainly. If a result is still unfolding, say that. If a page or video is really about the customer's situation, let it stay about the customer's situation.

sections.title: Know what one project can prove, and what it cannot
sections.body:
A customer project page is useful because it can show taste, judgment, and the shape of a real result. It is less useful when it pretends to settle every question at once. In my Cool Runnings work, the client reported a 30% increase in qualified bookings after the new website and local search system launched. That is worth discussing, but it is still one project, one business, and one set of circumstances. It is not a promise that every landscaping website will produce the same result in the same period.

The same is true for other kinds of work. With ABC Appliance, the useful part is the way the site clarifies service areas, appliance types, brand coverage, and what to expect before an appointment is confirmed. That is a real design and content decision with practical value. It still does not need a made up conversion figure attached to it. Good customer content builds trust by staying inside the evidence.

This is where restraint pays off. If you can say, "Here is the problem, here is what we did, here is what changed for this customer," that is enough. The reader can decide whether their situation is similar. If you need a broader answer, write it separately and label it honestly.

sections.title: Use a simple customer project worksheet
sections.body:
Before you draft the page, answer a few questions in a worksheet. That keeps the content useful instead of sentimental.

A practical worksheet for turning one customer project into website content
QuestionWhat to captureWhat to avoid
What was the customer's actual problem?Plain language in one or two sentences.Vague pain, buzzwords, or a problem you invented.
What limits shaped the work?Budget, timing, access, photography, season, local conditions.Pretending the project had no constraints.
What did you change or build?The concrete work, the pages, the media, the copy, the system.A fog of strategy words without visible work.
What changed afterwards?A specific client-reported change, a clearer enquiry pattern, or a useful business observation.Broad claims that one project cannot support.
Where should this live?Service page, local page, case study, video, or social.Creating a thin page because you feel you should.

If the answers are thin, that is still useful. It tells you to keep the story short, use a photo and one clear point, or wait for a better project. A lot of owners feel pressure to publish more proof than they have. Usually the better move is to publish less, but make it real.

sections.title: Make the decision once, then reuse the project well
sections.body:
The best customer project content usually comes from slowing down once and making a few clean choices. Who is this for? What did they need to understand? What can the work honestly prove? What belongs on the website, and what belongs in a sales conversation? Once those answers are clear, the same project can support a page, a video, a few images, and a useful social post without turning into a pile of half finished marketing pieces.

If you want a second set of eyes on how to frame a real project for your website, service pages, or broader brand, start a conversation. The best use of one good job is often much simpler, and much more useful, than people expect.

faqs: Should a customer project go on the service page or on a separate case study page?

If the project proves a repeatable part of your service, a section on the service page is often enough. Use a standalone case study when the project has enough detail, context, and decision making to reward a longer read.
Do I need customer video if I already have photos?
Not always. Photos may be enough if the work is simple and visual. Video becomes more useful when the story needs motion, voice, sequence, or a clearer explanation of what changed.
Can I use a customer project if I do not have hard numbers?
Yes, if you are honest about the limits. A clear description of the problem, constraints, work, and client-reported change can still be useful. Do not invent metrics to make the page feel stronger.
